Daniel’s most interesting move—linking his father’s oversimplifying narratives to “extremism,” and then linking his own extremism to a sparse value system—rests on a quiet conflation: *certainty* and *simplicity* are not the same thing as *extremity*. Oversimplification is often less about holding an extreme position than about collapsing a multidimensional problem into a single axis that feels legible; it can yield moderate conclusions just as easily as radical ones, and it can also be a social technology (keeping conversation fluent, protecting status, avoiding conflict) rather than a truth-claim. The sharper diagnostic isn’t “extremist” but “premature closure”: ending inquiry early because a coherent story has arrived. That frames Daniel’s “training” more clearly too—what he learned may be closer to rhetorical agility (producing plausible alternative stories) than to truth-tracking critical thinking, which more often looks like calibration, probabilistic language, and disciplined exposure to disconfirming evidence. This is why the best writing on “tolerating ambiguity” emphasizes not paralysis but *holding multiple models at once* and updating; it’s the spirit of Tetlock’s “fox” over “hedgehog” thinking (Daniel might recognize himself toggling between both) in works like *Superforecasting* ([Superforecasting](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/318891/superforecasting-by-philip-e-tetlock-and-dan-gardner/)).

The second hidden simplification is Daniel’s heavy-tail story: “modern life is heavy-tailed, therefore extremity is profitable.” Heavy tails do appear in venture returns and some scientific impact measures, but the inference “be extreme” skips the selection effects and survivorship bias that make the few winners visible and the many ruined experiments invisible. A heavy-tailed world doesn’t reward extremity in general; it rewards *asymmetric payoff structures* plus *a portfolio strategy that can survive losses*. Taleb’s point is not “be radical,” but “structure exposure so that downside is bounded and upside is open-ended” ([The Black Swan](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/176227/the-black-swan-by-nassim-nicholas-taleb/)). Translating that to research policy, the real question is less A vs. B than: what institutional designs preserve exploratory diversity *without* turning most labs into disposable lottery tickets—e.g., partial lotteries for high-risk grants, longer time horizons, and mechanisms that protect early-career researchers from catastrophic failure.

If Daniel wants to keep the essay’s psychological honesty while tightening the argument, a useful reframing is: the virtue isn’t “non-extremism,” it’s **strong hypotheses, weak identity**—strong opinions *loosely held*. That’s the bridge between his father’s soothing closure and his own self-described extremity: both can become identity armor. Ambiguity tolerance, in practice, is less a mood than a method—explicit uncertainty, reversible decisions where possible, and deliberate contact with the best version of the opposing case—so that the narrative remains a tool, not a cage.
